newsitem.title: TURKEY: Black Sea heads seek cooperation to end conflict.
newsitem.headline: Black Sea heads seek cooperation to end conflict.

text.p: Black Sea leaders were urged to embrace cooperation and unity as a way to combat regional conflicts at the start of a conference in Istanbul on Monday.

"The joint vision of all those gathered here is to see the Black Sea as a prosperous place of peace and stability, cleansed of tensions and clashes," Turkish President Suleyman Demirel told the opening session of the Black Sea Economic Cooperation (BSEC) grouping's two-day conference.

Demirel said many of the member countries -- Turkey, Greece, Moldova, Albania, Bulgaria, Romania, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Ukraine and Russia -- had turned their backs on each other and sometimes even been enemies.

"But today we are happy to see, as a result of this imaginative initiative, that this region's countries want to leave the past behind...that they are working hard and with determination to create a "Black Sea" vision where cooperation takes the place of conflict and disagreement," he said.
The gathering however, was preceded by turmoil in Albania and by some of the worst fighting in three years between Armenia and Azerbaijan.

The presidents of the latter two countries held talks in Istanbul ahead of the conference and Armenian President Levon Ter-Petrosyan said that a fragile ceasefire -- declared in 1994 -- remained in place despite the recent clashes.
"The ceasefire should continue as a good basis for peace and seeking mutually acceptable foundations for building peaceful cooperation in the area," Ter-Petrosyan said.
But Azeri President Haydar Aliyev said that the actions of Armenia went against the intended spirit of cooperation of the conference.

"As a result of acts by Armenia, 20 percent of Azerbaijan is currently occupied by Armenian forces and there are over a million refugees in our country," Aliyev said. "We call upon Armenia to act for a peaceful solution to the conflict and reconfirm Azerbaijan's commitment to a peaceful solution."
The two countries traded accusations of cross-border attacks last week after two weeks of sporadic and violent clashes.

BSEC officials have said that bilateral antagonism and lack of a private sector in some member states, and the troubled economies of ex-Soviet states, have hampered the group, but they hope to have a free trade zone in the region by 2010.

"Our country has proven to be an active presence in the process of creating a BSEC free trade area...We have already made a decisive step forward in this direction, by concluding the free trade agreement between Romania and Turkey which will be signed tomorrow," Romanian President Emil Constantinescu said.

Georgian President Eduard Shevardnadze compared the work of the conference leaders to that of canal builders. "But no builder can give the canals life-giving water. We must open the floodgates to private investment for that," Shevarnadze said.

BSEC, the brainchild of former Turkish President Turgut Ozal, was set up in 1992. But it has undertaken no projects so far, and conference organisers hope the Istanbul conference will come up with concrete plans.

Delegates include six heads of state, ministers of transport, economy and communication, representatives of the World Bank, the European Bank of Reconstruction and Development and the International Finance Corporation, and some 600 businessmen.
